steps.caption: Black to move. White's knight has just taken the pawn on e5, and the black bishop on g4 attacks the white queen. Is the queen free?

claims.statement: Bxd1 is a legal move: the bishop can take the queen.

steps.prompt: Before you see anything else: would you take the queen? Write your choice and the one thing you would check first.

fields.label: The first thing I would check:

steps.caption: Step through what happens if Black takes the queen.

line.say: Black takes the queen. On a count of material this wins nine points for a bishop.
White does not recapture. The bishop takes f7 with check, and the knight on e5 guards it.
The king cannot take a guarded bishop, so it steps to e7.
The knight arrives on d5 with checkmate. Black's own queen and bishop block the last squares.

claims.statement: Bxd1 is at least 1000 centipawns worse than the best move (depth 16): it walks into mate.

steps.caption: White to move. This is the position just before the mating move. Why can the king not run?

line.say: Checkmate. The bishop on f7 covers e8 and e6, the knight on e5 covers d7, and the knight on d5 covers f6.

claims.statement: Nd5 is checkmate.
Exactly one white piece, the bishop on f7, attacks e8.

steps.caption: Now the other side of the story: what Black should have played.

line.say: Black takes the knight with the pawn and refuses the queen. White's queen still attacks the bishop on g4.
The queen takes the bishop. White has won the pawn on e5, so Black is a pawn down and the engine rates it about two pawns worse (depth 16). Worse, but the game goes on.

claims.statement: dxe5 is the engine's first choice (depth 16).

steps.text: A **trap** is a **lure** plus a **hidden reply**. The lure here was a free queen, and the hidden reply was a check followed by mate. Black's bishop left g4 and ended on d1, far from the defence of its own king. The reply exists in the position before you take. So before any capture ask two things. What does it open or take away? What can the other side do next?

[R] The pattern is named after the Sire de Légal, who is credited with playing it against Saint Brie in Paris in 1750. That attribution is recalled, not checked here, and the moves are exactly the line on the first board.

steps.caption: Black to move. White took the pawn on e5 with the f-pawn. In our Lichess sample at 1100-1300, 113 of the 129 games that reached this position recaptured with the d-pawn (counts, not evaluations). Watch what the queen sees instead.

line.say: The queen checks along the diagonal that the f-pawn used to cover.
White blocks with the g-pawn, one natural way to meet a check.
The queen takes the e-pawn with check, and the rook on h1 is now attacked along the long diagonal.
White blocks again, this time with the queen.
The black queen takes the rook.

claims.statement: Qh4+ is the engine's first choice (depth 16).
Recapturing with the d-pawn is at least 250 centipawns worse than Qh4+ (depth 16).

steps.caption: White to move. Black's queen on g5 attacks the knight on e5 and the pawn on g2. In our 1100-1300 sample 430 games reached this position, and White chose the capture on f7 in 166 of them (39%).

line.say: The knight takes f7 and attacks both the queen on g5 and the rook on h8.
Black ignores the fork. The queen takes g2, attacking the rook on h1 and the pawn on e4.
White saves the rook.
The queen takes e4 with check.
White blocks the check with the bishop.
The knight gives mate. The bishop on e2 is pinned and cannot take it, and the king has no free square.

claims.statement: Nxf7 is at least 500 centipawns worse than the best move (depth 16).

steps.caption: Black to move. The finish of that line: the white king is boxed in by its own pieces.

line.say: The knight on d4 gives checkmate.

claims.statement: Nf3 is checkmate.

steps.caption: White to move. The pawn on d6 can take the knight on e7, and Black's bishop stands on c5.

line.say: The pawn takes a knight. If Black recaptures, White has won a piece for a pawn.
Black answers with a check and gives up the bishop.
The king takes the bishop. It no longer guards the queen.

The black queen takes the white queen along the d-file, which has no pawns left on it. White has lost the queen and a pawn for a knight and a bishop: the engine rates it about 3.5 pawns for Black (depth 16).

claims.statement: dxe7 is at least 400 centipawns worse than the best move (depth 16).
After dxe7 the black queen attacks the white queen on d1.
After Bxf2+ Kxf2 the white queen on d1 is loose: attacked and not defended.

steps.caption: White to move. Black's pawn on e3 has just taken a pawn, and the bishop on b4 stands attacked by the bishop on d2. Taking it looks like a free piece.

line.say: White takes the bishop that gave check. A piece looks won.
The pawn takes f2 with check, attacking the king and the knight on g1.
The king steps to e2. The pawn on f2 is still alive, and the next board shows what it does.

claims.statement: Bxb4 is at least 400 centipawns worse than the best move (depth 16).

steps.caption: Black to move. The pawn on f2 can promote on g1 by taking the knight. Which piece should it become? Two short boards follow to show why.

line.say: The pawn takes the knight and becomes a knight, with check.
The king goes back to e1.
The queen checks again. Black is far ahead, about 5.8 pawns by the engine (depth 16).

claims.statement: Promoting to a knight is the engine's first choice (depth 16).
Promoting to a queen is at least 300 centipawns worse (depth 16).

steps.caption: Black to move, the same position. First try the queen, the piece most players would pick.

line.say: The pawn takes the knight and becomes a queen, but it gives no check, so White has time.
White takes the black queen with check.
The king takes back.
The rook takes the new queen. The engine now says level (depth 16).

claims.statement: Promoting to a queen is at least 300 centipawns worse than the best move (depth 16).
After the queen promotion the white queen on d1 attacks the black queen on d8.

steps.caption: Black to move, the same position. Now the knight, and the reply a greedy White might try.

line.say: The pawn becomes a knight with check. White cannot take on d8 now, because the check must be answered first.
White takes the knight with the rook.
The bishop checks the king and attacks the queen behind it on d1.
The king steps away.
Black takes the queen. Black is about 9 pawns ahead by the engine (depth 16).

claims.statement: After Rxg1 Bg4+ the black bishop attacks the white queen on d1.
Promoting to a knight on g1 is a legal move.

steps.text: [I] Why the knight? The knight check leaves White no time for the queen trade, and the bishop on c8 is ready to join in. [H] Promotion to a knight is rare in play, so most learners never look for it. Whenever a pawn is one step from the end, ask which piece it should become, not only whether it can queen.

**Five traps, four shapes.** [I] This sorting is ours. The f-pawn capture **opened a line**. The knight capture ignored a **counter-threat**. The captures on e7 and b4 each met a **check in between** (Bxf2+, exf2+). The last was a **promotion**: a pawn near the end is a piece in disguise. Légal combines a check with mate. Name the shape and the reply is easier to find.

steps.caption: White to move, the position from the first of the last two boards. Here is how White declines the bait.

line.say: White takes the pawn on e3 with the f-pawn. That pawn was the one the trick needed, so the trick is gone.
Black has a check, but it is only a check.
White blocks, and the engine rates the game about level.

claims.statement: fxe3 is the engine's first choice (depth 16).
The position is within 0.6 pawns of equal (White's point of view, depth 16).

steps.caption: White to move. The pawn on d5 can be taken by the knight, and the bishop on g5 seems to make that safe. Here is the capture that White would regret.

line.say: White takes the pawn with the knight.
Black takes the knight with the other knight, and Black's queen is now attacked by the bishop on g5.
White takes the queen.
Black checks first, and the white queen must deal with it.
White blocks with the queen.
The bishop takes the queen with check.
The king takes the bishop.

Black takes back the bishop on d8. Count: Black lost a pawn, a queen and a bishop; White lost a knight, a queen and a bishop. Black is up a knight for a pawn, because the check came before the capture could count.

claims.statement: Nxd5 is at least 400 centipawns worse than the best move (depth 16).

steps.text: **Remember.** A trap is a lure that looks like a gain plus a hidden reply that your own capture makes possible. The reply may open a line, make a counter-threat, give a check in between, or come from a promotion. Before you capture, ask what the capture opens and what the other side can do next.
